analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $7.25 an hour by 2002.
analysis.headline: Ted Kennedy's bill to raise the minimum wage in five yearly steps to $7.25 never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Labor Committee and died there when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to lift the federal minimum wage in stages, from the then-current $5.15 to $5.65 in September 1998 and up to $7.25 by September 2002 [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Senator Edward Kennedy on July 11, 1997, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1][S3]. No further action was ever taken, and the bill expired when that Congress ended in January 1999 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers earning near the federal minimum would have seen paychecks rise in five annual steps to $7.25 an hour by 2002 [S2][S3]. At the time the bill was introduced the federal minimum stood at $5.15, so the bill represented roughly a 40% increase phased over four years, reaching workers in food service, retail, cleaning, and other low-paid hourly jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 in September 1998, $6.15 in 1999, $6.65 in 2000, $6.95 in 2001, and $7.25 in September 2002 [S2][S3].
The increase is phased in over four years, giving employers time to adjust while lifting pay for workers at or near the minimum [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers, concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service and manufacturing industries, would have borne higher payroll costs; some of that cost could have been passed to consumers through prices, and some economists predicted reduced hiring at the low end.

drawbacks.text: A phased increase to $7.25 was roughly a 40% rise over the then-current $5.15 floor; opponents argued such a jump could reduce entry-level hiring, cut hours, or push small employers toward automation [S2][S3].
The bill contained no small-business exemptions, tax offsets, or regional cost-of-living adjustments, so a single national floor applied equally to high-cost and low-cost areas [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of workers then earning between $5.15 and $7.25 an hour, the bill offered a direct, substantial raise phased in over four years. The main costs fell on the businesses employing them and possibly on some entry-level job opportunities, the standard trade-off in every minimum-wage debate. The bill was a straightforward raise with no complicating offsets, so its merits turn on the long-running empirical question of how much a 40% phased increase would have affected employment — evidence from later state and federal increases suggests the job losses were generally modest relative to the wage gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never reported it out, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced S. 1009 on July 11, 1997, and delivered introductory remarks [S1][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources (the labor committee then chaired by Jim Jeffords, R-VT) [S5].
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed, and the bill died in committee when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum-wage workers were spared the scheduled increases, and the $5.15 federal floor stayed in place until 2007, when the wage was finally raised in the 110th Congress. Low-wage workers got no raise from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage employers; low-wage workers got nothing

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Two Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Senate committee of referral (chaired by Jim Jeffords, R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to sit in committee for the remainder of the Congress; no floor consideration was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican majority's committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: Among the most minimum-wage-intensive industries, it would have faced the largest direct payroll increases. In killing the bill it kept labor costs at the 1996-97 level.

industries.industry: Retail trade and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Retail, cleaning, and other hourly-service employers would have borne the higher wage floor; the bill's failure preserved the status quo for them.
